notes.meaning: Jonathan listened to David speak with King Saul and felt an immediate bond with him. Both young men loved God deeply and shared great courage on the battlefield. Jonathan loved David with a pure and loyal friendship, valuing David as much as his own life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters suggest there was a romantic or homosexual bond between David and Jonathan, though the text describes a deep, loyal friendship.

notes.meaning: Saul brought David into his royal court on a permanent basis. David had previously divided his time between playing music for the king and tending his father's sheep. From this day forward, he lived at the palace full-time as a royal servant.

Jonathan formed a solemn agreement of lifelong brotherhood with David. To show his total loyalty, Jonathan took off his royal robe and handed over his weapons and belt. Since Jonathan was the crown prince, giving away his royal gear showed he gladly accepted that God had chosen David to be the next king.

Saul sent David on various military missions, and David acted with great wisdom and succeeded every time. Because of this success, Saul placed him over troops of soldiers. The general public and even the king's courtiers were delighted with David's new position.

When the army returned from defeating the Philistines, women from the towns came out singing, dancing, and playing instruments to welcome the soldiers. In their song, they chanted that Saul had killed thousands, while David had killed tens of thousands. This poetic comparison gave higher praise to David than to the king.

Saul became extremely angry at the women's song because they credited David with greater victories than him. He worried that the kingdom itself would soon be taken from him and given to David. From that day on, Saul watched David with suspicion, envy, and bitter hatred.

The very next day, God permitted a distressing spirit to trouble Saul, throwing him into an agitated fit where he raved wildly. David came in to soothe the king by playing his harp as he had done in the past. Saul sat listening while clutching a royal spear in his hand.

In a sudden burst of rage, Saul threw his spear at David, aiming to pin him to the wall. David moved quickly and escaped being struck on two separate occasions. Even though his life was threatened, David chose to trust God's protection rather than attack the king.
Saul realized he had good reason to fear David. The Lord was clearly helping David, while He had withdrawn His blessing from Saul. This spiritual contrast filled the king with deep dread.

Saul sent David away from the palace and placed him in charge of a unit of a thousand soldiers. Saul hoped this dangerous post would lead to David's death in battle, but David led his men faithfully. Everything David did turned out well because the Lord was with him.

Seeing David succeed at every turn made Saul even more afraid of him. At the same time, the people across all the tribes grew to love David because he bravely led them into battle and back home again. David's humble and capable leadership won the hearts of the whole nation.

Saul offered his oldest daughter, Merab, to David in marriage if David would fight the nation's enemies. Saul sounded generous, but he was setting a deadly trap. He secretly hoped the Philistines would kill David in battle so he would not have to murder David himself.

David answered Saul with sincere humility rather than ambition. He asked who he or his family were that he should be honored as a son-in-law to the king. David did not suspect the trap and spoke out of genuine lowliness.

When the time came for Merab to marry David, Saul broke his royal promise. Instead of giving her to David, Saul gave her as a wife to a man named Adriel. This sudden change was a severe insult to David, yet David accepted it quietly.

Saul learned that his younger daughter, Michal, had fallen in love with David, and the news pleased him. He saw this as a second chance to lure David into a fatal situation against the Philistines. Saul then told David he had another opportunity to become the king's son-in-law.

Because David was cautious after being mistreated regarding Merab, Saul ordered his palace officials to talk to him in private. They were told to assure David that the king liked him and that all the servants supported the marriage. This flattery was meant to coax David into accepting the match.

David told the officials that marrying a princess was no small matter, pointing out that he was a poor man who could not pay a suitable bride price. An ancient bride price was a gift of money or goods given to the bride's father before marriage. When the servants reported David's humble words back to Saul, the king prepared his answer.

Saul told his servants that he wanted no money for the bride price, only the foreskins of one hundred dead Philistines as payback against the enemy. This requirement served as proof that the slain men were truly uncircumcised enemies and not fellow Israelites. Saul's real goal was to send David into extreme danger where the Philistines would kill him.

David was glad to accept these terms because he could win a bride and serve his nation without needing great wealth. Before the set deadline passed, David and his men went out and killed two hundred Philistines, doubling what the king had asked. David delivered the full count to Saul, leaving the king with no choice but to give Michal to him in marriage.

Saul had to face the undeniable truth that the Lord was actively protecting David and that Michal truly loved her new husband. These facts did not lead Saul to repent; instead, they made him dread David even more. From that time forward, Saul remained David's determined enemy.

Whenever the Philistine commanders marched out to attack Israel, David outmatched all of Saul's other officers in wisdom and military skill. His continued victories brought safety to God's people. As a result, David gained an honorable reputation and was held in the highest regard throughout the land.
